summary: MPLS Network Actions are technologies that indicate actions affecting how a packet is forwarded or monitored along its label switched path, with any extra data needed. This informational RFC describes an architectural framework for MNA.

eli5.summary: A parcel can carry sticky notes saying "do this at each stop." This lays out the overall plan for how network packets can carry such instructions.

subtitle: A framework for letting an MPLS packet carry instructions, and the data they need, inside its label stack.

tldr.problem: MPLS routers forward packets by looking at labels, but there is no common way for a packet to ask routers to do something extra, such as monitoring it, and to carry the data that action needs.
tldr.mechanism: The framework defines a Network Action Sub-Stack (NAS): a run of label stack entries that starts with a special-purpose label and holds action indicators and ancillary data, optionally followed by post-stack data. It lists the design choices a concrete solution must make.
tldr.outcome: It is an architecture, not a wire format. Solutions must choose an encoding and specify ordering, scope and handling of unknown actions. The RFC is Informational and has been updated by RFC 9994.

facts.label: Action scopes
facts.value: Hop by Hop, Ingress to Egress, Select

today: RFC 9789 is an Informational framework and has been updated by RFC 9994, which is the place to look for the later requirements on documents that define network actions. The RFC itself assigns one IANA code point: IGP MSD-Type 3, Readable Label Depth.

sections.title: Why Network Actions
sections.content:
An MPLS router normally forwards a packet by its label. MPLS forwarding actions already exist, for example load-balancing a packet using its entropy, or indicating whether to perform Fast Reroute on a failure. This framework widens the idea to network actions: anything an MPLS router is asked to do with a packet, including security functions and Operations, Administration, and Maintenance (OAM) procedures that are not directly about forwarding.

The solutions built on this framework are meant to meet the requirements in RFC 9613. A network action is always triggered by an MNA packet, but it may affect later traffic, including packets that are not MNA packets.
sections.eli5: Routers usually just read the address on a parcel and pass it on. This document lets a parcel also carry extra notes that say 'please do this one more thing while you handle me'.

sections.title: The Network Action Sub-Stack
sections.content:
Network actions and their data live in a Network Action Sub-Stack (NAS): a set of related, contiguous label stack entries (LSEs). Its first entry, the Network Action Sub-Stack Indicator (NSI), carries a special-purpose label called the MNA label. A NAS can then hold Network Action Indicators (NAIs), which say which actions are present, and In-Stack Data (ISD), which is the ancillary data for those actions. The meaning of the Label, TC and TTL fields inside a NAS may be redefined, but the meaning of the S bit does not change.

Putting the data deeper in the stack means routers must look past the first LSE. The RFC notes that this was first introduced with the Entropy Label. Some actions may instead put data after the stack, called post-stack data. In both cases the order of the data follows the order of the indicators, and a solution must give an unambiguous order in which the actions are applied.

The framework assumes the MPLS working group will pick a single solution for encoding in-stack data and not more than one for post-stack data.
sections.eli5: Think of a stack of cards. The first special card says 'notes start here', and the next cards hold the notes and any extra information. Routers read down into the stack to find them.

sections.title: Scopes, Unknown Actions and Signaling
sections.content:
An action can have one of three scopes: Hop by Hop (every node along the path performs it), Ingress to Egress (only the last node performs it), or Select (only specific nodes do). A solution that supports Select must say how the nodes are chosen. The framework does not limit which scope an action may use.

Devices may not know every action. Legacy devices that do not recognize the MNA label will discard the packet if it is the top label. For unknown actions, a solution must choose how to proceed: stop processing, drop the packet, or perform the known actions and ignore the rest. Capabilities are assumed to be signaled by other protocols, with per-action granularity.

One piece of signaling is defined here: Readable Label Depth (RLD), the number of LSEs from the top of the stack that a router can read with no performance impact. A node that pushes a NAS must make sure that every node expected to process it can read the whole NAS within its RLD. RLD is advertised with IGP MSD-Type value 3.
sections.eli5: Some notes say 'everyone do this', some say 'only the last stop do this', and some name particular stops. A stop that does not understand a note must follow a rule for what to do, such as skipping it or throwing the parcel away.

sections.title: Encoding Choices
sections.content:
The framework lays out options rather than picking one. For the MNA label, a solution may reuse an existing base special-purpose label, take a new base or extended one, or let operators define the label, which adds management overhead. The first LSE of a NAS uses 20 bits of Label and the Bottom of Stack bit, which could leave 11 bits (the 3-bit TC and 8-bit TTL) for MNA purposes.

A solution also needs a way to find the end of the NAS, either a continuation bit in each LSE or a fixed-size Length field. To say which actions are present, it may use a bit catalog (one bit per action, efficient when many actions are present) or operation codes (a fixed number of bits per action, efficient when few are present). The RFC compares them: choosing only the 256th action takes 256 catalog bits but just 8 opcode bits.

Post-stack data raises a first nibble question. The first nibble after the label stack is already used by other mechanisms, so a post-stack solution must specify its contents and how it interacts with other uses.
sections.eli5: There are several ways to write the notes. A checklist with a tick box per action is short when many ticks are needed. A list of code numbers is short when you only need one or two things.

sections.title: Defining a Network Action
sections.content:
The framework requires a deterministic order for processing the actions in a packet, and each action must say how it interacts with all previously defined actions. Private network actions, which are not publicly documented, must still be included in the ordering.

A document that defines a network action must give its Name, its Network Action Indicator (bit position or opcode), its Scope, its State effects, whether it is Required or Optional, and the encoding of any In-Stack Data and Post-Stack Data. If that data has variable length, the solution must show how to find its length without implementing the action. A solution should create an IANA registry for network actions. Management sections must also describe how to diagnose networks that use MNA.
sections.eli5: Anyone who invents a new kind of note must fill in a form: its name, how to mark it, who should obey it, and how much extra information comes with it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points out that the MPLS forwarding plane has no built-in security mechanisms, so network operational security is central. Link-level security such as MACsec stops covert observation of the label stack, which matters because MNA information may be sensitive.

MNA adds one risk that a solution SHOULD address. If one network's MPLS traffic is carried over a second MPLS network by pushing more LSEs, MNA information from the first network may be visible to MNA-capable forwarders in the second and cause unpredictable behavior. Mitigations are to reject MNA information that does not come from a trusted network, or to fully encapsulate the inbound packet in a new label stack. The RFC rejects as unsafe the idea of pushing enough labels to hide third-party MNA data below the RLD.
sections.eli5: If someone else's sticky notes get mixed into your parcel, your stops might obey them by mistake. So the rules say to block outside notes or wrap the parcel in fresh packaging.

viz.caption: THE THREE SCOPES OF A NETWORK ACTION

items.title: Hop by Hop
items.text: Every node along the path performs the action.

items.title: Ingress to Egress
items.text: Only the last node on the path performs the action.

items.title: Select
items.text: Only specific nodes along the path perform the action.
